newsitem.title: USA: North Dakota urges FERC to back coal gas plant.
newsitem.headline: North Dakota urges FERC to back coal gas plant.

text.p: North Dakota's lawmakers on Wednesday urged the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to ensure that the Great Plains coal gasification plant in their state remains open.

The $2 billion coal-to-natural gas plant, conceived in the aftermath of the 1973 oil crisis, would have to close if the commission endorses an administrative law judge's decision which rejected settlements on prices paid by pipelines for synthetic natural gas from the plant, the three Democratic lawmakers and Dakota Gasification Co officials said.
"Closing the plant would undermine our national energy interests and would create a serious setback in this country's move towards energy independence," Sen. Kent Conrad said at a commission hearing.
Commissioners called for the extraordinary hearing because the plant has been linked to broad energy policies, and closing it down would hurt U.S. taxpayers and the local economy.

Dakota Gasification attorneys said the company could not afford to keep the plant running if the pipeline settlements were overturned and it had to pay refunds of $270 million to pipeline customers who had contested the settlements.

Taxpayers have a stake in the case because the plant -- the world's only commercial coal gasification plant -- was taken over in 1985 by the Energy Department, when the original owners defaulted on $1.5 billion in government-backed loans.
The Energy Department sold the plant to Basin Electric Power Cooperative, Dakota Gasification's parent company, for $85 million and a share of future synthetic gas sales revenue.
The government stands to lose $45 million in cash and some sales revenue if the pipeline settlements are rejected, Energy Department general counsel Robert Nordhaus said.

Commissioners' questioning suggested they were looking for a way to keep the plant open, generating revenue from sales of synthetic natural gas and a range of byproducts including fertilizer, while also appeasing the pipelines' customers.
